topic: Siachen and NJ9842, where the Line of Control stops
hook: Your map of the Line of Control stops at a point called NJ9842, and nobody wrote down exactly where it goes next.
title: Why Siachen Is Stranger Than You Think
description:
The Line of Control on your map stops at a point called NJ9842, and the 1949 agreement only says it runs 'thence north to the glaciers'. This video walks through six true facts about Siachen: how a vague sentence became the highest battlefield on Earth, the 1984 race for the ridges, the brutal cold, and one soldier's six days under the snow. Watch to the end to see why that gap on the map is still open today.

#Siachen #LineOfControl #StrangeFacts
comment_prompt: Would you ever visit Siachen base camp: yes or no?

chapters.title: The Gap That Is Still Open

scenes.narration: Your map of the Line of Control stops at a point called NJ9842, and nobody wrote down exactly where it goes next.
scenes.headline: The Map Just Stops

scenes.narration: That missing stretch sits on the highest battlefield on Earth, where soldiers have died for decades, mostly from cold and snow.
scenes.headline: Highest Battlefield

scenes.narration: By the end, you'll see six strange facts about Siachen, and the last one explains why this gap is still open.
scenes.headline: Six Strange Facts

scenes.narration: Stay for the final fact, because it comes down to five words written in 1949 and never fixed.
scenes.headline: Five Words, 1949

scenes.narration: First, let's find that point. Open any map of India and Pakistan and follow the Line of Control north.
scenes.headline: Follow The Line

scenes.narration: The line crawls through the mountains of Kashmir, and then, near the top, it simply stops.
scenes.headline: Then It Stops

scenes.narration: That is not a printing error in your atlas. That is exactly how the agreement was written.
scenes.headline: Not A Printing Error

scenes.narration: Fact one: a real border on a real map ends at a spot called NJ9842, and then it just stops.
scenes.headline: Fact One

scenes.narration: NJ9842 is a map grid reference, a tiny dot high in the Karakoram mountains.
scenes.headline: A Tiny Dot

scenes.narration: It comes from the Karachi Agreement of 1949, signed by Indian and Pakistani army officers after the first war over Kashmir.
scenes.headline: Karachi Agreement

scenes.narration: United Nations military observers were sent to watch over that ceasefire line.
scenes.headline: UN Observers

scenes.narration: They marked the ceasefire line carefully, point by point, all the way up to NJ9842.
scenes.headline: Point By Point

scenes.narration: After that point, the agreement says only one thing: the line runs thence north to the glaciers.
scenes.headline: North To The Glaciers

scenes.narration: Read that again. No coordinates, no peaks, no valleys. Just north, to the glaciers.
scenes.headline: Just North

scenes.narration: Why so vague? The usual explanation is simple: nobody believed anyone would ever want that frozen land.
scenes.headline: Nobody Wanted It

scenes.narration: In 1972, after another war, the Simla Agreement set up the Line of Control, and the line still ended at NJ9842.
scenes.headline: Simla, 1972

scenes.narration: So one of the most watched borders in the world has a loose end, hidden in plain sight on a map.
scenes.headline: A Loose End

scenes.narration: Let's see how that loose end turned into a fight.
scenes.headline: From Gap To Fight

scenes.narration: Fact two: the argument did not start with soldiers. It started with maps and mountain climbers.
scenes.headline: Fact Two

scenes.narration: The words north to the glaciers can be read in more than one way, and the two countries read them differently.
scenes.headline: Two Readings

scenes.narration: India says the line should follow the natural watershed, along a mountain wall called the Saltoro Ridge.
scenes.headline: India: Saltoro Ridge

scenes.narration: Pakistan's reading, shown on some maps, runs the line from NJ9842 toward the Karakoram Pass instead.
scenes.headline: Pakistan: Karakoram Pass

scenes.narration: Between those two lines lies the Siachen Glacier, over seventy kilometres long, one of the longest glaciers outside the polar regions.
scenes.headline: Siachen Glacier

scenes.narration: In the late 1970s, Pakistan gave permits to foreign climbers to explore the glacier.
scenes.headline: Climbing Permits

scenes.narration: Some Western maps then began drawing the border straight across to the Karakoram Pass, which put Siachen on Pakistan's side.
scenes.headline: Maps Changed

scenes.narration: India saw those maps and permits as a quiet claim on the ice, and decided it could not wait.
scenes.headline: A Quiet Claim

scenes.narration: The Indian Army sent its own mountaineering expeditions up the glacier to show it was watching.
scenes.headline: India Climbs Too

scenes.narration: Notice how strange that is. A fight over a glacier was built from climbing permits and the way a map was drawn.
scenes.headline: A Fight Over Ink

scenes.narration: And the name itself is gentle. Siachen is often translated as place of wild roses.
scenes.headline: Place Of Roses

scenes.narration: Roses, on a glacier where almost nothing grows. And the next fact is where the story turns serious.
scenes.headline: It Gets Serious

scenes.narration: Fact three: in April 1984, two armies raced for ridges and passes around eighteen thousand feet high.
scenes.headline: The Race, 1984

scenes.narration: On the thirteenth of April, India launched Operation Meghdoot, named after the cloud messenger in an old Sanskrit poem.
scenes.headline: Operation Meghdoot

scenes.narration: Helicopters lifted Indian soldiers onto the heights, because there was no road and no easy path on foot.
scenes.headline: Lifted By Helicopter

scenes.narration: India took the main passes along the Saltoro Ridge: Sia La, Bilafond La and Gyong La.
scenes.headline: Three Key Passes
scenes.sub: Sia La, Bilafond La, Gyong La

scenes.narration: Reports say Pakistan was preparing its own move, and found Indian troops already holding the high ground.
scenes.headline: Days Too Late

scenes.narration: Since then, India has held the high ridge, and Pakistan holds positions lower down on the other side.
scenes.headline: High Ground, Low Ground

scenes.narration: Pakistan tried to push back in 1987, and a post was later renamed Bana Top after Bana Singh, who won the Param Vir Chakra.
scenes.headline: Bana Top

scenes.narration: That post sits well above twenty thousand feet, higher than most people ever climb in their lives.
scenes.headline: Above 20,000 Feet

scenes.narration: Think about that. Two armies fought for land with no farms, no villages and no roads.
scenes.headline: Land Nobody Lived On

scenes.narration: If you enjoy strange maps and places like this, subscribe, because we post a new one every day.
scenes.headline: New Strange Place Daily

scenes.narration: In the end, the race was won in days, but holding the ridge has taken decades.
scenes.headline: Days To Win, Decades To Hold

scenes.narration: Now, what is life up there actually like?
scenes.headline: Life Up There

scenes.narration: Because the real enemy on Siachen was never the other army.
scenes.headline: The Real Enemy

scenes.narration: Fact four: the weather on Siachen has killed far more soldiers than gunfire ever did.
scenes.headline: Fact Four

scenes.narration: Temperatures at the posts can fall to around minus fifty degrees Celsius in winter.
scenes.headline: Minus Fifty

scenes.narration: Blizzards can last for days and bury a tent overnight.
scenes.headline: Tents Buried

scenes.narration: At that height there is far less oxygen, so even walking ten steps can leave you breathless.
scenes.headline: Thin Air

scenes.narration: Frostbite is a daily danger, and touching bare metal in that cold can tear your skin.
scenes.headline: Frostbite

scenes.narration: Some posts can only be reached by helicopter, and bad weather can cut them off for days.
scenes.headline: Cut Off For Days

scenes.narration: Deep cracks called crevasses hide under fresh snow, so soldiers walk roped together.
scenes.headline: Hidden Crevasses

scenes.narration: Indian soldiers first train at a high-altitude school in Ladakh, to let their bodies adjust before they go up.
scenes.headline: Siachen Battle School

scenes.narration: Tours at the highest posts are kept short, because the body wears down in that thin, freezing air.
scenes.headline: Short Tours

scenes.narration: In 2012, an avalanche buried a Pakistani army camp at Gayari, and more than a hundred soldiers died.
scenes.headline: Gayari, 2012

scenes.narration: No battle did that. A mountain of snow slid down in seconds.
scenes.headline: Snow, Not Shells

scenes.narration: And one survival story from Siachen sounds so unlikely that it feels made up.
scenes.headline: Almost Unbelievable

scenes.narration: Fact five: in February 2016, an avalanche hit an Indian army post at Siachen and buried ten soldiers.
scenes.headline: Fact Five

scenes.narration: Rescuers dug for days in the freezing cold, using dogs and detection equipment to search the snow.
scenes.headline: Digging For Days

scenes.narration: On the sixth day, they found Lance Naik Hanumanthappa Koppad alive, under many feet of snow.
scenes.headline: Found Alive

scenes.narration: He was barely conscious, but he was breathing, kept alive in a small pocket of air under the snow.
scenes.headline: A Pocket Of Air

scenes.narration: He was flown to an army hospital in Delhi, and for a few days the whole country prayed for him.
scenes.headline: A Country Prayed

scenes.narration: Sadly, he died on the eleventh of February, but his story shows how brutal this land is.
scenes.headline: 11 February

scenes.narration: The other nine soldiers buried with him did not survive.
scenes.headline: Nine Others Lost

scenes.narration: Remember, every one of these stories sits on one unfinished sentence from 1949.
scenes.headline: One Unfinished Sentence

scenes.narration: Which brings us to the biggest fact of all, and it is about right now.
scenes.headline: The Biggest Fact

scenes.narration: Fact six: more than seventy-five years later, the line is still not defined past NJ9842.
scenes.headline: Fact Six

scenes.narration: India and Pakistan have held talks about Siachen over many years, and reports say they came close to a deal more than once.
scenes.headline: Talks, Again And Again

scenes.narration: Pulling troops back sounds simple, but each side wants today's positions written down first, and that has been the sticking point.
scenes.headline: The Sticking Point

scenes.narration: In November 2003, the two countries agreed a ceasefire, and the guns on Siachen have been largely quiet since.
scenes.headline: Ceasefire, 2003

scenes.narration: So today it is a frozen standoff, with soldiers living at the top of the world just to hold a position.
scenes.headline: A Frozen Standoff

scenes.narration: In 2019, India opened the area from Siachen base camp up to Kumar Post to tourists.
scenes.headline: Open To Tourists

scenes.narration: The glacier matters beyond politics. Its meltwater feeds the Nubra River, which flows into the Shyok and then the Indus.
scenes.headline: Source Of Rivers

scenes.narration: Studies say Siachen has been shrinking over the years.
scenes.headline: Glacier Shrinking

scenes.narration: Waste left by decades of soldiers adds to the damage, which makes the glacier's future a new kind of dispute.
scenes.headline: Decades Of Waste

scenes.narration: So the question has changed. It is not only who owns the glacier, but what will be left of it.
scenes.headline: What Will Be Left

scenes.narration: Now go back to the start. Your map of the Line of Control stops at NJ9842.
scenes.headline: Back To NJ9842

scenes.narration: Beyond it, the agreement says only: thence north to the glaciers.
scenes.headline: Thence North

scenes.narration: Five words, one dot on a map, and one of the toughest places humans have ever fought over.
scenes.headline: Five Words, One Dot

scenes.narration: No farms, no villages, no roads, and still two armies stayed, all because one sentence was left unfinished.
scenes.headline: One Unfinished Sentence

scenes.narration: That is why Siachen is stranger than you think. The world's highest battlefield began with a gap on a map.
scenes.headline: A Gap On A Map

scenes.narration: Tomorrow: the country whose clock is exactly fifteen minutes ahead of India's.
scenes.headline: Next: Fifteen Minutes
